title: Even Here
subtitle: A 'cautionary tale' walking guide through the Holocaust in the country that thought it knew better…

modal.heading: Why "Even Here"?

sections.heading: A cautionary tale
sections.body: The Anne Frank story most of us know — the swinging bookcase, the helpers, "in spite of everything" — is a true story. It is also one story, and the one we tell ourselves most often. What this walk wants you to know is what that comforting version leaves out.

sections.heading: What the comforting story leaves out
sections.body:
There were 101,996 other Jews deported from the Netherlands. There were 220 Sinti and Roma names. There were the gay men remembered at the Homomonument, the Sephardic community of the Esnoga, the resistance dead of the Population Register attack, the Indonesian dead held in the urn at the Dam.

The Netherlands had the highest Jewish-victim percentage in Western Europe — about 75 % — produced not by occupiers alone but by a civil service that registered the names, a city government that mapped the addresses, a railway that ran the trains, and a population that, with notable exceptions, watched. The Dutch state apologised for this in 2020. The Dutch railways paid restitution in 2019. These reckonings are recent.

sections.heading: Why "the country that thought it knew better"
sections.body:
The Netherlands had centuries of self-image as Europe's tolerant exception — Spinoza's city, refuge for Sephardic Jews fleeing Iberia in the 1490s, refuge for German Jews fleeing Hitler in the 1930s. Tolerance was the brand.

Tolerance turned out to be brittle when tested by occupation, paperwork, and apathy. A country that imagines itself unlike Germany or Poland or Russia is not, by virtue of that self-image, unlike them. That is why this walk is a cautionary tale — for the Netherlands, and for any society that mistakes its own civility for safety.

sections.heading: What this walk does
sections.body:
Anne Frank's annex stays at Stop 2. The other sixteen stops are the city around it: events she lived through in Amsterdam (the first Razzia in February 1941, when she was eleven; the February strike that followed it; the deportations of 1942–43, which her family went into hiding to escape on 6 July 1942), events she did not live to see (the Groote Club shooting on 7 May 1945, three months after her death at Bergen-Belsen in February 1945; the liberation she missed by weeks), and the memorials — almost all of them built decades later — that try to keep what happened from being forgotten.

The Names Monument at Stop 16 was unveiled in 2021. Anne is one of the 102,220 names carved there. Even here is the phrase each of these stops completes. Even in Spinoza's city. Even in the country of refuge. Even in the Amsterdam of the diary and the bookcase. Even here, this happened. It can happen anywhere.

modal.closing: May their memory be a blessing.
